title: Effect of ketogenic diets on insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-1 in humans: A systematic review and meta-analysis - ScienceDirect
abstract:
Effects of 2-year calorie restriction on circulating levels of IGF-1, IGF-binding proteins and cortisol in nonobese men and women: a randomized clinical trial
Effects of 2-year calorie restriction on circulating levels of IGF-1, IGF-binding proteins and cortisol in nonobese men and women: a randomized clinical trial
Intra-individual pre- and post-comparisons were prioritized over inter-individual comparisons to account for the broad variability in clinically standard circulating IGF-1 levels. The outcome included the measurement of circulating IGF-1 levels (primary outcome of this review) and optional measurements of circulating glucose and insulin levels (secondary outcomes). The study designs included human interventional studies including randomized and non-randomized clinical trials and excluded observational studies, non-interventional studies, animal studies, and in vitro studies.
In contrast, moderate calorie restriction without protein restriction does not affect IGF-1 levels (Fontana et al., 2008b, Fontana et al., 2016b). There is a pressing requirement to assess the long-term safety, tolerability, and adherence of KDs across various patient cohorts (Zhu et al., 2022, Chen et al., 2023). In clinical settings, KDs have been safely implemented for up to 20 weeks (Kämmerer et al., 2021) and have shown compatibility with aggressive radiotherapy regimes (Klement et al., 2020b, Klement et al., 2021, Klement et al., 2022).
The extracted data for each eligible study included: author, year, demographics, study design, population health condition, sample size, intervention description and duration, intended and achieved caloric and macronutrient intakes, weight changes, as well as mean and standard deviation of serum levels of IGF-1, glucose and insulin at baseline and post-intervention time points. All data were extracted using Excel. Median, interquartile range and/or standard error of the mean (SEM) were extracted where mean and standard deviation were not reported. Risk of bias assessments were independently performed by four reviewers (GR, MLC, TW or AYP). For randomized clinical trials (RCTs), the Cochrane Collaboration's tool for Risk of Bias Assessment Tool 2.0 (RoB2) (Higgins et al., 2011) was utilized.
